An ASSUMPTION gives its basis.\n32\t\n33\t**Missing inputs:** the unknowns that would change the plan most, and any assumption the phase\n34\torder rests on.\n35\t\n36\t## 2. {"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"toolu_bdrk_01R8k4sZ94pMeUkFrLJj42cs","type":"tool_result","content":"1\t# Worked examples: dependencies, validation gates, labels, reversibility, budgets, exceptions\n2\t\n3\tExamples for the rules in `SKILL.md`. This file adds no rules of its own. The tables mix different\n4\tsystems on purpose; they are not one plan.\n5\t\n6\t## 1. Dependency kinds\n7\t\n8\t| Kind | Software | Infra | AI / agentic |\n9\t|---|---|---|---|\n10\t| Structural | invoicing builds on the ledger schema | clusters build on the network + IAM baseline | the retrieval index builds on the chunk schema + metadata |\n11\t| Runtime | the API needs the identity provider up | deploys need DNS and the registry up | the answer path needs the model endpoint and vector store up |\n12\t| Decision | keys, schema, and billing wait on the tenancy model | the credential model waits on pull vs push deploys | the data pipeline waits on prompt+RAG vs fine-tune |\n13\t| Validation | the partitioning scheme waits on \"one primary sustains peak\" | the runner-fleet design waits on \"hosted runners meet the queue-time target\" | answer tuning waits on \"retrieval finds the supporting passage\" |\n14\t| Risk / security | an external beta waits on authorization + tenant isolation | prod admission waits on signed artifacts | agent write access waits on injection containment + a tool allow-list |\n15\t| Organizational | live card payments wait on the acquirer confirming PCI scope | the prod cutover waits on a change-board slot | training on customer data waits on a legal review of data use |\n16\t| Economic | the pricing model waits on payment fees per transaction | the retention policy waits on storage growth | general availability waits on cost per resolved conversation |\n17\t\n18\tCommon misses:\n19\t\n20\t- Treating \"the service starts\" as evidence that it sustains the load.\n21\t- Discovering a lead time (security review, vendor contract, data-processing agreement, production\n22\t  account) in launch week — or, worse, in week one of Phase 0.\n23\t- Scaling an AI feature before cost per resolved conversation is measured on real traffic.\n24\t- Ordering by code imports while a decision is still open, so the code is rewritten when it lands.\n25\t\n26\t## 2. Validation gates\n27\t\n28\tFour independent examples, each from a different system.\n29\t\n30\t| | V1 Capacity (validation) | V2 Retrieval (AI) | V3 PCI scope (risk/security + organizational) | V4 Inference cost (economic) |\n31\t|---|---|---|---|---|\n32\t| **Hypothesis** | One Postgres primary carries the projected write load at the 12-month data size | For answerable questions, the index returns a supporting passage in the top 5 | Card entry only in the provider's hosted fields keeps our PCI DSS scope at SAQ A (reduced, not zero) | Answers cost less per resolved conversation than the human handling they replace |\n33\t| **Method** | Benchmark at 2× projected peak on data sized to the 12-month projection, long enough to include autovacuum and checkpoints | ≥ 200 labeled real questions with known source passages, per index version | Data-flow review against SAQ A eligibility, confirmed with the acquirer or a QSA | Meter cost per turn on shadow traffic, then cost per resolved conversation on a 5% canary for one week |\n34\t| **Acceptance threshold** | p99 commit < 50 ms at 2,000 writes/s (ASSUMPTION: projected peak 1,000 writes/s) | hit rate@5 ≥ 0.90 (ASSUMPTION; about ±4 points of sampling error at 200 questions) | Acquirer or QSA sign-off: no card number is stored, processed, or transmitted by our systems; a PAN scan of logs and databases finds none | UNKNOWN: needs the human cost per ticket from the support lead, before Phase 4 |\n35\t| **Evidence** | Benchmark report stored with the build | Eval report in CI for each index version | Completed SAQ A and attestation of compliance | Cost dashboard export for the canary week |\n36\t| **Unlocks (and if it fails)** | A single-primary data model with sharding deferred; if it fails, the partitioning decision opens | Prompt and answer-format tuning; if it fails, re-chunk or change the embedding model before tuning | Taking live card payments; if it fails, re-scope the card flow | General availability; if it fails, narrow the rollout or route more to humans |\n37\t\n38\tShadow traffic alone cannot measure cost per resolved conversation: users never see the answers,\n39\tso the follow-up turns and resolutions never happen. That is why V4 needs a canary.\n40\t\n41\tA good acceptance threshold:\n42\t\n43\t- is a number with its conditions (load, data shape, duration, sample size) when the property is\n44\t  measured, or a named reviewer's pass/fail sign-off on a stated question when it is a design,\n45\t  security, or legal judgment;\n46\t- carries its label: REQUIREMENT, BASELINE, ASSUMPTION (with its basis), or UNKNOWN (no number);\n47\t- can fail within the phase that owns it, and is wider than its own sampling noise;\n48\t- has a consumer: if nothing downstream changes when it fails, it is an exit check, not a gate.\n49\t\n50\tAnti-patterns:\n51\t\n52\t- **\"Proven because it runs.\"** Running shows the path exists, not that it is fast, safe,\n53\t  correct, or affordable enough.\n54\t- **A number labeled UNKNOWN.** \"99.9% (UNKNOWN)\" is invented precision with a disclaimer. An\n55\t  UNKNOWN has no number.\n56\t- **Validation theater.** Gates on R1 decisions, gates nobody consumes, or a gate for every AI\n57\t  sublayer.\n58\t- **Evidence as a result.** \"Benchmark showed 42 ms\" in a plan written before any benchmark ran.\n59\t- **Evidence that leaks.** A parity or benchmark report that copies regulated records into CI;\n60\t  store identifiers or counts, not the records.\n61\t\n62\t## 3. Reversibility\n63\t\n64\t| Tier | Examples |\n65\t|---|---|\n66\t| **R1** | A library behind an interface, internal naming, log message wording, UI styling, the test runner |\n67\t| **R2** | Queue technology (R3 if it is the system of record and consumers rely on replay), ORM, an internal service boundary, cache topology, the CI system, a structured log schema once alerts or SIEM rules parse it, the UI framework, fine-tuning a model (weeks of data and eval work; a hosted fine-tune is tied to one provider's base model) |\n68\t| **R3** | The data model and identifiers once real data exists, tenancy and isolation, the consistency model, a public API with consumers you cannot update in lockstep, trust boundaries, data residency, data gravity at a vendor, training on customer or personal data (removable only by retraining) |\n69\t\n70\tCost of being wrong: making a storage bucket public is one click to undo, but the exposure cannot\n71\tbe undone, so the change is gated like R3. A cutover with rehearsed reverse replication is cheap to\n72\tundo, but the hour it runs wrong can lose or double-book records, so it is gated as an\n73\tirreversible operation.\n74\t\n75\tBasis instead of a gate: \"One Postgres primary at about 50 writes/s, roughly 100× below a single\n76\tprimary's limits\" needs no benchmark gate; \"standard practice\" alone is not a basis.\n77\t\n78\tSeams that turn R3 into R2 when the plan builds them: expand/contract schema migrations; an\n79\tinterface in front of the vendor's API plus a tested export of your data in an open format; the\n80\traw event log, with a retention policy and per-subject keys if it holds personal data; dual-write\n81\tthrough an outbox or change data capture, with a backfill and a reconciliation check; a tenant ID\n82\ton every row from day one.\n83\t\n84\t## 4. Budgets\n85\t\n86\t| Budget | Target | Label | Checked by |\n87\t|---|---|---|---|\n88\t| Latency | Time to first token p95 < 2 s; complete answer p95 < 6 s | ASSUMPTION: typical for hosted-LLM chat; confirm with the product owner | V0 records the floor; Phase 3 exit check at peak |\n89\t| Throughput | 50 requests/s at peak | REQUIREMENT: stated in the request | Phase 2 load test |\n90\t| Availability / SLO | — | UNKNOWN: needs the availability the business commits to (product owner, before Phase 4); a model API, vector store, and database in series at 99.9% each cap it near 99.7% unless fallback answers count as available | SLIs and burn-rate alerts at Phase 4; attainment over the first 30 days |\n91\t| AI inference cost | — | UNKNOWN: needs the human cost per ticket (support lead, before Phase 4) | V4 |\n92\t| Operational complexity | One service and one managed database; no self-hosted cluster | ASSUMPTION: a two-person team | Phase 3 exit check |\n93\t\n94\tRows that do not bind are left out (here, storage cost). Unknowns are fine; fabricated certainty\n95\tis not. The walking skeleton measures the first real values, and later gates check against them.\n96\t\n97\t## 5. Methodology exceptions\n98\t\n99\t| ID | Rule bypassed | Why it does not apply | Replacement validation | Evidence required | Resumes when |\n100\t|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n101\t| E1 | Walking skeleton first (principle 6) | Feasibility is the main risk: nobody knows whether a model can extract invoice fields accurately enough | Two-week offline spike on 300 labeled invoices covering the vendor and layout mix; proves extraction quality only, so integration and deployment risk stay open | Spike report: accuracy per critical field (total, due date, bank details) and the share of invoices needing no correction (thresholds ASSUMPTION) | The spike passes and Phase 0 builds the production skeleton; if it fails, re-scope or stop |\n102\t| E2 | Skeleton runs in production (principle 6) | Certified medical device: nothing reaches production before clearance | Skeleton runs in a production-equivalent environment on target hardware, under design controls | Verification records traceable into the submission | Permanent for the certified scope: every release passes change control, and a significant change needs re-submission unless an approved change-control plan covers it; uncertified back-office tools follow the normal order |\n103\t| E3 | Dependency order (principle 1) | A regulatory date fixes when the reporting feature ships, before its data source is validated | Build behind a flag against the source's contract, with contract tests, and keep an interim manual report that meets the date | Contract tests pass against the real source, and report totals reconcile with the system of record | The source's validation gate passes; the feature is re-checked before exposure |\n104\t| E4 | Cross-cutting moves in every phase (principle 5) | Throwaway prototype answering one product question in two weeks | Containment instead of hardening: synthetic or consented data only, no production credentials or network path, a separate account, a teardown date | The decision record, and the teardown done or the re-plan started | The prototype is chosen to become a product: re-plan from Step 1 |\n105\t\n106\tNot exceptions:\n107\t\n108\t- \"N/A — <reason>\" for something that does not exist in this system.\n109\t- Brownfield work. Example of the normal method: a CI/CD platform for 50 services takes one real\n110\t  service through the new platform to production in Phase 0, with its old pipeline kept as the\n111\t  fallback, and migrates the rest in waves.\n112\t- Reading principle 6 for software you do not operate: a CLI's skeleton is the released package,\n113\t  installed the way users install it, renaming a real folder in dry-run mode (writes run on a\n114\t  disposable copy until the undo journal's gate passes).\n115\t- Data-protection regimes (HIPAA, PCI DSS, GDPR). This file adds no rules of its own. The tables mix different\nsystems on purpose; they are not one plan.\n\n## 1. Dependency kinds\n\n| Kind | Software | Infra | AI / agentic |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Structural | invoicing builds on the ledger schema | clusters build on the network + IAM baseline | the retrieval index builds on the chunk schema + metadata |\n| Runtime | the API needs the identity provider up | deploys need DNS and the registry up | the answer path needs the model endpoint and vector store up |\n| Decision | keys, schema, and billing wait on the tenancy model | the credential model waits on pull vs push deploys | the data pipeline waits on prompt+RAG vs fine-tune |\n| Validation | the partitioning scheme waits on \"one primary sustains peak\" | the runner-fleet design waits on \"hosted runners meet the queue-time target\" | answer tuning waits on \"retrieval finds the supporting passage\" |\n| Risk / security | an external beta waits on authorization + tenant isolation | prod admission waits on signed artifacts | agent write access waits on injection containment + a tool allow-list |\n| Organizational | live card payments wait on the acquirer confirming PCI scope | the prod cutover waits on a change-board slot | training on customer data waits on a legal review of data use |\n| Economic | the pricing model waits on payment fees per transaction | the retention policy waits on storage growth | general availability waits on cost per resolved conversation |\n\nCommon misses:\n\n- Treating \"the service starts\" as evidence that it sustains the load.\n- Discovering a lead time (security review, vendor contract, data-processing agreement, production\n  account) in launch week — or, worse, in week one of Phase 0.\n- Scaling an AI feature before cost per resolved conversation is measured on real traffic.\n- Ordering by code imports while a decision is still open, so the code is rewritten when it lands.\n\n## 2. Validation gates\n\nFour independent examples, each from a different system.\n\n| | V1 Capacity (validation) | V2 Retrieval (AI) | V3 PCI scope (risk/security + organizational) | V4 Inference cost (economic) |\n|---|---|---|---|---|\n| **Hypothesis** | One Postgres primary carries the projected write load at the 12-month data size | For answerable questions, the index returns a supporting passage in the top 5 | Card entry only in the provider's hosted fields keeps our PCI DSS scope at SAQ A (reduced, not zero) | Answers cost less per resolved conversation than the human handling they replace |\n| **Method** | Benchmark at 2× projected peak on data sized to the 12-month projection, long enough to include autovacuum and checkpoints | ≥ 200 labeled real questions with known source passages, per index version | Data-flow review against SAQ A eligibility, confirmed with the acquirer or a QSA | Meter cost per turn on shadow traffic, then cost per resolved conversation on a 5% canary for one week |\n| **Acceptance threshold** | p99 commit < 50 ms at 2,000 writes/s (ASSUMPTION: projected peak 1,000 writes/s) | hit rate@5 ≥ 0.90 (ASSUMPTION; about ±4 points of sampling error at 200 questions) | Acquirer or QSA sign-off: no card number is stored, processed, or transmitted by our systems; a PAN scan of logs and databases finds none | UNKNOWN: needs the human cost per ticket from the support lead, before Phase 4 |\n| **Evidence** | Benchmark report stored with the build | Eval report in CI for each index version | Completed SAQ A and attestation of compliance | Cost dashboard export for the canary week |\n| **Unlocks (and if it fails)** | A single-primary data model with sharding deferred; if it fails, the partitioning decision opens | Prompt and answer-format tuning; if it fails, re-chunk or change the embedding model before tuning | Taking live card payments; if it fails, re-scope the card flow | General availability; if it fails, narrow the rollout or route more to humans |\n\nShadow traffic alone cannot measure cost per resolved conversation: users never see the answers,\nso the follow-up turns and resolutions never happen. That is why V4 needs a canary.\n\nA good acceptance threshold:\n\n- is a number with its conditions (load, data shape, duration, sample size) when the property is\n  measured, or a named reviewer's pass/fail sign-off on a stated question when it is a design,\n  security, or legal judgment;\n- carries its label: REQUIREMENT, BASELINE, ASSUMPTION (with its basis), or UNKNOWN (no number);\n- can fail within the phase that owns it, and is wider than its own sampling noise;\n- has a consumer: if nothing downstream changes when it fails, it is an exit check, not a gate.\n\nAnti-patterns:\n\n- **\"Proven because it runs.\"** Running shows the path exists, not that it is fast, safe,\n  correct, or affordable enough.\n- **A number labeled UNKNOWN.** \"99.9% (UNKNOWN)\" is invented precision with a disclaimer. An\n  UNKNOWN has no number.\n- **Validation theater.** Gates on R1 decisions, gates nobody consumes, or a gate for every AI\n  sublayer.\n- **Evidence as a result.** \"Benchmark showed 42 ms\" in a plan written before any benchmark ran.\n- **Evidence that leaks.** A parity or benchmark report that copies regulated records into CI;\n  store identifiers or counts, not the records.\n\n## 3. Reversibility\n\n| Tier | Examples |\n|---|---|\n| **R1** | A library behind an interface, internal naming, log message wording, UI styling, the test runner |\n| **R2** | Queue technology (R3 if it is the system of record and consumers rely on replay), ORM, an internal service boundary, cache topology, the CI system, a structured log schema once alerts or SIEM rules parse it, the UI framework, fine-tuning a model (weeks of data and eval work; a hosted fine-tune is tied to one provider's base model) |\n| **R3** | The data model and identifiers once real data exists, tenancy and isolation, the consistency model, a public API with consumers you cannot update in lockstep, trust boundaries, data residency, data gravity at a vendor, training on customer or personal data (removable only by retraining) |\n\nCost of being wrong: making a storage bucket public is one click to undo, but the exposure cannot\nbe undone, so the change is gated like R3. A cutover with rehearsed reverse replication is cheap to\nundo, but the hour it runs wrong can lose or double-book records, so it is gated as an\nirreversible operation.\n\nBasis instead of a gate: \"One Postgres primary at about 50 writes/s, roughly 100× below a single\nprimary's limits\" needs no benchmark gate; \"standard practice\" alone is not a basis.\n\nSeams that turn R3 into R2 when the plan builds them: expand/contract schema migrations; an\ninterface in front of the vendor's API plus a tested export of your data in an open format; the\nraw event log, with a retention policy and per-subject keys if it holds personal data; dual-write\nthrough an outbox or change data capture, with a backfill and a reconciliation check; a tenant ID\non every row from day one.\n\n## 4. Budgets\n\n| Budget | Target | Label | Checked by |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Latency | Time to first token p95 < 2 s; complete answer p95 < 6 s | ASSUMPTION: typical for hosted-LLM chat; confirm with the product owner | V0 records the floor; Phase 3 exit check at peak |\n| Throughput | 50 requests/s at peak | REQUIREMENT: stated in the request | Phase 2 load test |\n| Availability / SLO | — | UNKNOWN: needs the availability the business commits to (product owner, before Phase 4); a model API, vector store, and database in series at 99.9% each cap it near 99.7% unless fallback answers count as available | SLIs and burn-rate alerts at Phase 4; attainment over the first 30 days |\n| AI inference cost | — | UNKNOWN: needs the human cost per ticket (support lead, before Phase 4) | V4 |\n| Operational complexity | One service and one managed database; no self-hosted cluster | ASSUMPTION: a two-person team | Phase 3 exit check |\n\nRows that do not bind are left out (here, storage cost). Unknowns are fine; fabricated certainty\nis not. The walking skeleton measures the first real values, and later gates check against them.\n\n## 5. Methodology exceptions\n\n| ID | Rule bypassed | Why it does not apply | Replacement validation | Evidence required | Resumes when |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| E1 | Walking skeleton first (principle 6) | Feasibility is the main risk: nobody knows whether a model can extract invoice fields accurately enough | Two-week offline spike on 300 labeled invoices covering the vendor and layout mix; proves extraction quality only, so integration and deployment risk stay open | Spike report: accuracy per critical field (total, due date, bank details) and the share of invoices needing no correction (thresholds ASSUMPTION) | The spike passes and Phase 0 builds the production skeleton; uncertified back-office tools follow the normal order |\n| E3 | Dependency order (principle 1) | A regulatory date fixes when the reporting feature ships, before its data source is validated | Build behind a flag against the source's contract, with contract tests, and keep an interim manual report that meets the date | Contract tests pass against the real source, and report totals reconcile with the system of record | The source's validation gate passes; the feature is re-checked before exposure |\n| E4 | Cross-cutting moves in every phase (principle 5) | Throwaway prototype answering one product question in two weeks | Containment instead of hardening: synthetic or consented data only, no production credentials or network path, a separate account, a teardown date | The decision record, and the teardown done or the re-plan started | The prototype is chosen to become a product: re-plan from Step 1 |\n\nNot exceptions:\n\n- \"N/A — <reason>\" for something that does not exist in this system.\n- Brownfield work. {"type":"assistant","message":{"model":"claude-opus-5-5","id":"msg_bdrk_em3jxtyekxe6gr6fx4krbbui45bbtphlygf3xss7dur46mkijsva","type":"message","role":"assistant","content":[{"type":"text","text":"# BUILD PLAN: Multi-tenant SaaS billing platform\n\n> **Assumptions this plan rests on** (stated because the request doesn't settle them, and two of them change the phase order):\n> **(a)** This is a billing *platform*: each tenant (a SaaS company) uses it to bill its own end customers for subscriptions and usage. It is not the billing module of a single SaaS product that bills its own tenants. If it is the module, buy Stripe Billing or Chargebee, and Phase 5 plus most of §3 drops out.\n> **(b)** Tenants are the merchant of record, charging through their own connected payment-provider accounts. We never hold funds. If we become the merchant of record, the plan goes back to Step 1, because licensing and tax registration then come first.\n> **(c)** It is greenfield, and usage-based pricing is needed at launch. If it isn't, Phase 4 moves to §10.\n\n## 1. Classification and constraints\n- **What:** A multi-tenant billing platform. Tenants set up a catalog and subscriptions and report usage. The platform rates usage, issues invoices, collects payment through a payment provider (PSP), runs dunning (retrying failed payments), and keeps a double-entry ledger.\n- **Type:** Software on managed cloud infra. Greenfield. Not a small build: outside tenants, money, and end-customer personal data.\n- **Dominant constraint:** Correctness, meaning money and tenant isolation.\n- **Worst failure:** Money moves wrongly and nobody notices before settlement: an end customer is charged twice, charged the wrong amount, or charged under the wrong tenant.\n\n**Budgets**\n\n| Budget | Target | Label | Checked by |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Correctness | 0 ledger imbalances; 0 duplicate or wrong-amount charges; 0 reconciliation breaks still unexplained after 2 business days | ASSUMPTION: follows from the worst failure; the finance lead confirms | V1, V4 |\n| Latency | API p99 < 300 ms on paths that don't call the PSP; usage ingest acknowledged in p99 < 100 ms | ASSUMPTION: tenants call these inline from their own signup and metering paths; design partners confirm | V0 records the floor; V3 |\n| Throughput | — | UNKNOWN: needs tenant count, end customers, invoices/month and peak usage events/s at 12 months. Product owner supplies it, before Phase 2 | V3 |\n| Invoice run window | All invoices for a closed period finalized within 4 h of period close | ASSUMPTION: invoices should land before the tenant's next business day | V3 |\n| Availability / SLO | — | UNKNOWN: needs the SLA we commit to tenants. Business owner, before Phase 5. Design rule regardless: the PSP is never in the serial path of ingest or reads | Phase 6 SLO alerts |\n| RPO / RTO | RPO 0 for ledger, invoices and accepted usage events; RTO 1 h | ASSUMPTION: money records can't be re-derived. Uses Multi-AZ managed Postgres with synchronous storage replication | Phase 2 restore drill; Phase 6 DR drill |\n| Storage / retention | Raw usage events: 13 months hot, then object storage | ASSUMPTION (hot window). Legal retention period is UNKNOWN: depends on tenant jurisdictions; legal supplies it before Phase 6 | Phase 6 |\n| Unit cost per invoice | — | UNKNOWN: needs the target take rate. Business owner, before Phase 6. Measured from Phase 3 (PSP platform fees, tax-engine calls, infra) | Phase 6 exit |\n| Operational complexity | 2 deployables (billing core, usage ingest), managed Postgres, managed queue; no self-hosted clusters | ASSUMPTION: one team of 5–8 | Phase 6 exit |\n\n**Missing inputs:**\n1. Assumption (a): platform vs module.\n2. Assumption (b): who is merchant of record.\n3. Volume projections, which V3 needs.\n4. Pricing models required at launch: flat, per-seat, tiered, usage, prepaid.\n5. Launch markets. These drive tax, data residency and licensing (V6).\n6. Tenant SLA.\n7. Named finance lead and security reviewer.\n8. Two design-partner tenants.\n\n## 2. Dependency map\n\n| What waits | Depends on | Kind | Blocked from being |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Phase 0 PSP tier | PSP platform account approved (e.g. Stripe Connect platform); contract includes a token-portability clause | organizational | built (Phase 0) |\n| Every schema, key, query and auth path | Tenancy and isolation model (§3) | decision | specified |\n| Invoicing, payments and rating logic | V1: ledger and money math are correct | validation | specified |\n| Partitioning and usage-pipeline technology | Volume projection (input 3), then V3 | organizational → validation | hardened |\n| Any live card charge, including internal | V5: PCI scope stays at SAQ A | risk/security + organizational | exposed |\n| Live charging for external tenants | V4: no duplicate or wrong charges under faults | risk/security | exposed |\n| Any external tenant | V2 (isolation and pentest) and V6 (legal: funds flow, DPA, residency) | risk/security + organizational | exposed |\n| Live tax on invoices | Tax-engine contract; tenants' own tax registrations, which tenants supply | organizational | exposed |\n| Public API v1 freeze | V7: design partners integrate without breaking changes | validation + organizational | committed |\n| A tenant switching off its legacy billing | V8: shadow-run parity for that tenant | risk/security (irreversible) | committed |\n| Our pricing to tenants | Unit cost per invoice (§1) | economic | committed |\n\nEvery kind has at least one instance. Structural and runtime dependencies are left out because the phase order already shows them.\n\n## 3. Tradeoff gates (resolved up front)\n\n| Decision | Reversibility | Default (chosen now) | Assumption | Validated by | Flip condition |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| Tenancy and isolation | R3: rework of every row and query; a leak can't be undone | Pooled: one Postgres schema. `tenant_id` leads every primary key and index. Postgres Row-Level Security reads `app.tenant_id`, which is set per transaction from the authenticated context. Tenants are routed through a cell field so they can move to dedicated cells later | No tenant contractually needs physical isolation; volume fits one primary | V2, V3 | V2 fails, V3 fails, or a contract requires a dedicated database or region → that tenant moves to a silo cell |\n| Auth model and trust boundary | R3: trust boundary | Each request resolves to exactly one tenant at the edge: hashed, scoped API key, or OIDC session plus RBAC role. `tenant_id` is never read from the request body. Support staff get tenant-scoped, audited impersonation only | A single-tenant principal covers all use cases (no cross-tenant users at launch) | V2 | Agencies or resellers need multi-tenant principals → add an explicit membership model |\n| Ledger and data model | R3: identifiers and financial records once real data exists | Append-only double-entry ledger is the system of record for balances. Money is `bigint` minor units plus ISO 4217 currency. IDs are prefixed UUIDv7 (`inv_`, `cus_`). Prices are versioned and immutable. A finalized invoice never changes; corrections go through credit notes. Invoice numbers are gapless per tenant series, assigned at finalization | Postgres holds the ledger at projected volume | V1, V3 | V1 fails → redesign before dependents. V3 fails → partition the ledger by tenant and month, or use a dedicated ledger store (e.g. TigerBeetle) |\n| Consistency vs availability | R3: consistency model | Strong (serializable or row-locked transactions on one primary) for ledger, invoice finalization and payment attempts. Usage ingest favors availability: accept, store durably, rate later | Ingest volume is within reach of the stores in the usage-pipeline row | V3 | V3 shows ingest can't stay strongly consistent at peak → keep it eventual and use a stream store (usage-pipeline row) |\n| Monolith vs services | R2: internal boundary | Modular monolith (billing core) plus a separate usage-ingest service, because ingest has a different scale and uptime profile | One team owns the core | Phase 4 exit check | A module's scale or team ownership diverges |\n| Sync vs async | R2 | Synchronous commands with required idempotency keys. Invoice runs, payment attempts, dunning and outbound webhooks go async through a transactional outbox and a Postgres-backed job queue. Inbound PSP webhooks go through an inbox dedup table | Workflow complexity stays manageable without a workflow engine | Outbox crash test (Phase 1 exit) | Dunning or retry logic outgrows job tables → Temporal (§10) |\n| Usage pipeline | R2: data migration | Ingest writes to day-partitioned Postgres tables, unique on (`tenant_id`, `event_id`), then aggregates | Sustained peak stays under ~5k events/s (design parameter) | V3 | V3 projects above it → Kinesis/MSK plus ClickHouse behind the same ingest API |\n| Build vs buy | R3 for the PSP (stored payment methods live at the vendor); R2 for tax | Build the billing core (it is the product). Buy the PSP: Stripe Connect behind a `PaymentProvider` adapter, with payment methods held in the tenant's own connected account. Buy tax: Stripe Tax or Avalara behind a `TaxEngine` adapter. Buy OIDC/SSO (WorkOS or Auth0) | Stripe covers the launch markets' payment methods; the token-export clause is signed | V5; contract clause (§2) | A required market or method isn't covered → Adyen for Platforms through the same adapter |\n| Data-privacy boundary | R3: personal data | Card data never touches our systems (PSP-hosted fields). End-customer personal data sits in dedicated columns, encrypted with per-tenant data keys (KMS envelope encryption). Logs and traces carry IDs only. We act as processor under a DPA | Assumption (b) holds; tenants are controllers | V5, V6 | V6 changes our role → re-plan from Step 1 |\n| Funds flow / merchant of record | R3: legal | Tenant is merchant of record through connected accounts; we never hold funds; our fee is an application fee | No money-transmitter or payment-institution licence is needed in the launch markets | V6 | V6 fails → the PSP's managed-platform model, or re-plan |\n| Data residency | R3 | One home region, with `region` on the tenant record and in routing from day one | No launch market requires in-country storage | V6 | V6 or a tenant contract requires it → regional cell |\n| Public API contract | R3: outside consumers | Versioned REST with date-based versions pinned per tenant; idempotency keys on every POST; signed (HMAC), at-least-once webhooks carrying event IDs | Design partners can build on it | V7 | V7 fails → revise before freezing v1 |\n\n**R1 defaults:**\n- Language: Kotlin/JVM, chosen once before the first commit.\n- CI: GitHub Actions. IaC: Terraform. Runtime: AWS ECS Fargate with Aurora PostgreSQL Multi-AZ.\n- Telemetry: OpenTelemetry to any backend.\n- Feature flags: OpenFeature plus a vendor.\n- PDF rendering and the email provider sit behind interfaces.\n\n**N/A:** AI rows (no AI component). Brownfield migration rows (greenfield); migrating each tenant off its old billing is handled by V8.\n\n## 4. Walking skeleton (Phase 0)\n- **Request:** Internal tenant 0 (our own company, with an internal test customer) calls `POST /v1/subscriptions` with an idempotency key for a flat $1/month price. The call returns a subscription. A test clock advances the period; the invoice is finalized and charged. `GET /v1/invoices/{id}` then returns `paid`, and tenant 0's webhook endpoint receives `invoice.paid`.\n- **Tiers crossed:**\n  1. Edge: ALB plus WAF\n  2. API-key auth, which resolves the tenant\n  3. Billing core: subscription, invoice and ledger modules\n  4. Aurora Postgres, RLS on from the start\n  5. Outbox and job worker\n  6. PSP in **test mode**\n  7. Inbound webhook receiver\n  8. Ledger settlement\n  9. Outbound webhook dispatcher\n- **Day zero:**\n  - Deployed by GitHub Actions to ECS: images pinned by digest, Terraform-managed, migrations run in the pipeline.\n  - One OpenTelemetry trace runs from the API through the database, outbox, worker and PSP call to the webhook.\n  - Structured logs carry IDs only.\n  - Alerts on outbox lag, worker error rate, and failed webhook signatures.\n  - Rollback is redeploying the previous image. Migrations only add things.\n- **Who can reach it:** Only allow-listed tenant-0 API keys, behind a flag. No external tenants. The PSP runs in test mode, so no real money moves until V5 and V4 pass.\n- **Organizational tasks that start now:**\n  - PSP platform application and contract\n  - V5 and V6 reviews\n  - Volume projection (input 3)\n  - Name the finance lead and security reviewer\n  - Recruit two design partners\n\nExit check V0: §6.\n\n## 5. Phases\n\n- **Phase 1: Tenancy, identity, ledger and contracts** (widest rework first)\n  - Unlocks: Specifying everything that sits on the data model.\n  - Depends on: V0.\n  - Tasks:\n    1. Tenant, user, role and API-key model; OIDC dashboard login.\n    2. RLS policies on every table; a connection with no tenant context sees nothing.\n    3. ID scheme and money type.\n    4. Ledger accounts, transactions and entries, with a database-enforced balance invariant.\n    5. Invoice state machine (draft → finalized → paid / void / uncollectible).\n    6. Credit-note model.\n    7. Outbox and inbox tables; versioned event schemas.\n    8. Append-only audit log.\n    9. Per-tenant data keys for personal data.\n    10. Automated cross-tenant test suite (V2, part 1).\n    11. Ledger property tests (V1).\n  - Rollback: Only tenant-0 data exists, so the schema can still be rebuilt. From the end of this phase, migrations must be expand-then-contract and ledger corrections must be compensating entries.\n  - Exit check: V1 passes. V2 part 1 is green in CI. Killing the worker between commit and outbox dispatch produces neither a lost nor a duplicated event.\n\n- **Phase 2: Catalog, subscriptions and invoicing**\n  - Unlocks: Correct invoices for flat, per-seat and tiered prices.\n  - Depends on: Phase 1, V1, volume input 3.\n  - Tasks:\n    1. Products and immutable price versions.\n    2. Subscription lifecycle: create, upgrade or downgrade with proration, pause, cancel.\n    3. Billing clock and scheduler, with test clocks.\n    4. Invoice run: idempotent per (subscription, period), resumable, failures isolated per tenant.\n    5. Gapless numbering at finalization.\n    6. Tax-engine adapter in sandbox.\n    7. PDFs in a private bucket with short-lived signed URLs; email sending to an allow-list only.\n    8. V3 load test of the ledger and the invoice run.\n    9. Point-in-time restore drill.\n  - Rollback: A flag per pricing model. A finalized invoice can't be undone except by credit note, which is why only tenant 0 gets invoices.\n  - Exit check: V3 (ledger and run part) passes. The restore drill meets RPO/RTO. Expected vs generated invoices per period reconcile to 0 missing.\n\n- **Phase 3: Payments and collections**\n  - Unlocks: Collecting money.\n  - Depends on: Phase 2, V1; V5 before the first live charge.\n  - Tasks:\n    1. `PaymentProvider` adapter.\n    2. Connected-account onboarding.\n    3. Payment-method capture through PSP-hosted fields only.\n    4. Payment attempts whose PSP idempotency key is derived from `payment_attempt_id`.\n    5. Inbound webhook verification and inbox dedup.\n    6. Dunning schedule; refunds; disputes.\n    7. Daily reconciliation: every PSP balance transaction ↔ a ledger entry.\n    8. Duplicate-charge detector.\n    9. Kill switches for charging, one global and one per tenant.\n    10. V4 fault-injection suite in test mode, then live mode for tenant 0 only (employee cards, small amounts) for 2 cycles.\n  - Rollback: Kill switch plus PSP refunds. A captured live charge is a point of no return, guarded by V5 and V4.\n  - Exit check: V5 and V4 pass.\n\n- **Phase 4: Usage metering and rating**\n  - Unlocks: Usage-based and hybrid pricing.\n  - Depends on: Phase 2 (invoice lines), V1, V3 projection.\n  - Tasks:\n    1. Separate ingest service with tenant-scoped keys, per-tenant rate limits and quotas, and size limits.\n    2. Dedup on (`tenant_id`, `event_id`).\n    3. Late-event policy: events accepted until invoice finalization, then credited to the next period.\n    4. Aggregation, and a rating engine whose version is recorded on each invoice line.\n    5. Accepted-vs-rated reconciliation per tenant.\n    6. Dead-letter queue.\n    7. V3 ingest part, including node-kill tests.\n  - Rollback: Ingest flag per tenant. Unfinalized usage can be re-rated, because raw events are immutable and rating is deterministic.\n  - Exit check: V3 (ingest part) passes. A billing-core outage doesn't drop accepted events. If ingest and core don't separate cleanly, revisit the monolith-vs-services row.\n\n- **Phase 5: Tenant surface and first external tenant** (smallest exposure first)\n  - Unlocks: Real outside tenants.\n  - Depends on: Phases 3–4, V2 (pentest), V4, V6.\n  - Tasks:\n    1. Public API v1 release candidate.\n    2. Per-tenant sandbox (test mode) on the production version.\n    3. Tenant dashboard with SSO/MFA.\n    4. Hosted invoice and customer-portal pages.\n    5. Webhook delivery log, retries, and secret rotation.\n    6. External pentest (V2, part 2).\n    7. DPA signed.\n    8. Design partners integrate in sandbox (V7).\n    9. Design partner 1 goes live in **shadow**: invoices computed but not sent, their legacy billing stays the system of record. Compare for one cycle (V8).\n    10. Cut over design partner 1, then partner 2.\n  - Rollback: Until V8 passes, the tenant's legacy billing remains the system of record and we stay in shadow. After cutover, the tenant gets a full export (JSON/CSV). Their payment methods already sit in their own PSP account.\n  - Exit check: V2, V6, V8 pass for both partners. V7 is under way.\n\n- **Phase 6: General availability (GA) in waves**\n  - Unlocks: General onboarding.\n  - Depends on: Phase 5, V7, V8 per tenant, SLA and unit-cost inputs.\n  - Tasks:\n    1. Freeze API v1.\n    2. Waves of 1 → 5 → 25 → open, each pausable.\n    3. SLOs with burn-rate alerts, on-call and runbooks.\n    4. DR drill to RTO.\n    5. Retention and deletion jobs, once the legal period is known.\n    6. Access reviews.\n    7. Unit-cost dashboard against the target take rate.\n  - Rollback: Pause a wave or a tenant. Each tenant's decommissioning of legacy billing is a point of no return, guarded by V8 and that tenant's sign-off.\n  - Exit check: SLO attainment over the first 30 days. Unit cost is under the target. Operational complexity is within the budget.\n\n## 6. Validation gates\n\n| ID | Hypothesis | Method | Acceptance threshold | Evidence | Unlocks (and if it fails) | Phase |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| V0 | A change can be deployed, observed and rolled back through every tier in production | Run the §4 request; deploy, then roll back through the pipeline; kill the worker and send a bad webhook signature | The request succeeds with one trace across all tiers; deploy and rollback succeed; both injected failures fire alerts; first p99, outbox-lag and finalize-time values are recorded as baselines | Trace ID, pipeline run links, alert records, baseline sheet in the repo | Phase 1. AI layer\nN/A: no AI component.\n\n## 9. Methodology exceptions\nNone. Phase 0 runs in production with the PSP in test mode. Walking skeleton (Phase 0)\n- **Request:** Internal tenant 0 (our own company, with an internal test customer) calls `POST /v1/subscriptions` with an idempotency key for a flat $1/month price. A test clock advances the period; the invoice is finalized and charged. `GET /v1/invoices/{id}` then returns `paid`, and tenant 0's webhook endpoint receives `invoice.paid`.\n- **Tiers crossed:**\n  1. Edge: ALB plus WAF\n  2. API-key auth, which resolves the tenant\n  3. Billing core: subscription, invoice and ledger modules\n  4. Aurora Postgres, RLS on from the start\n  5. Outbox and job worker\n  6. PSP in **test mode**\n  7. Inbound webhook receiver\n  8. Ledger settlement\n  9. Outbound webhook dispatcher\n- **Day zero:**\n  - Deployed by GitHub Actions to ECS: images pinned by digest, Terraform-managed, migrations run in the pipeline.\n  - One OpenTelemetry trace runs from the API through the database, outbox, worker and PSP call to the webhook.\n  - Structured logs carry IDs only.\n  - Alerts on outbox lag, worker error rate, and failed webhook signatures.\n  - Rollback is redeploying the previous image. Migrations only add things.\n- **Who can reach it:** Only allow-listed tenant-0 API keys, behind a flag. No external tenants. The PSP runs in test mode, so no real money moves until V5 and V4 pass.\n- **Organizational tasks that start now:**\n  - PSP platform application and contract\n  - V5 and V6 reviews\n  - Volume projection (input 3)\n  - Name the finance lead and security reviewer\n  - Recruit two design partners\n\nExit check V0: §6.\n\n## 5. Phases\n\n- **Phase 1: Tenancy, identity, ledger and contracts** (widest rework first)\n  - Unlocks: Specifying everything that sits on the data model.\n  - Depends on: V0.\n  - Tasks:\n    1. Ledger accounts, transactions and entries, with a database-enforced balance invariant.\n    5. Invoice state machine (draft → finalized → paid / void / uncollectible).\n    6. Credit-note model.\n    7. Outbox and inbox tables; versioned event schemas.\n    8. Append-only audit log.\n    9. Per-tenant data keys for personal data.\n    10. Killing the worker between commit and outbox dispatch produces neither a lost nor a duplicated event.\n\n- **Phase 2: Catalog, subscriptions and invoicing**\n  - Unlocks: Correct invoices for flat, per-seat and tiered prices.\n  - Depends on: Phase 1, V1, volume input 3.\n  - Tasks:\n    1. PDFs in a private bucket with short-lived signed URLs; email sending to an allow-list only.\n    8. V3 load test of the ledger and the invoice run.\n    9. After cutover, the tenant gets a full export (JSON/CSV). Their payment methods already sit in their own PSP account.\n  - Exit check: V2, V6, V8 pass for both partners. Freeze API v1.\n    2. Waves of 1 → 5 → 25 → open, each pausable.\n    3. SLOs with burn-rate alerts, on-call and runbooks.\n    4. DR drill to RTO.\n    5. Retention and deletion jobs, once the legal period is known.\n    6. Access reviews.\n    7. Unit-cost dashboard against the target take rate.\n  - Rollback: Pause a wave or a tenant.
